about: The stage's story, as data (stage/stage.js reads it). One scene tells one story; each step adds one thing and is cumulative. From Dinis's arc to storytelling.1 (12 Nov 2026, 01:18 UTC): the five altitudes; the same privileges; policies; runs that cannot reach the asset; the mesh against one agent per asset; scale; cost. Numbers come from the run files; scenes on sim: graphs are labelled SIMULATED on screen. storytelling.1 and swarm.1.designer may edit this file: keys are documented in stage/README.md.

scenes.title: Mandate, reach, gap
scenes.say: Three words for the rest of the demo. Mandate: what a unit is asked to do. Reach: what its process can actually touch. The gap between them is where things go wrong.
scenes.cue: Reach is measured: swarm.1's own container, before any policy (harness E01, 01:37 UTC).

scenes.title: A send button is not a mandate
scenes.say: RiskMandate's published findings on Gmail and Calendar: the grants are user-shaped, so an agent that may draft may also send, and an agent that may edit your calendar can do damage nobody can undo.

card.title: A send button is not a mandate
lines: Mandate: read and draft, never send. Grant: includes send, behind a setting the account can flip.
“The narrowest permission that lets it read one message lets it read every message.”
Calendar keeps deleted events for 30 days, and documents no way to get back an edited one.
A line in the agent's instructions is “a rule in prose, enforced by nobody.”

scenes.say: A real run, on a simulated database: made-up suppliers and invoices (storytelling.1, 01:59 UTC). The mandate: pay invoice INV-002, 250, once. scenes.title: Run it where the assets are not
scenes.say: A real run from tonight. The agent only commits a signed request; a GitHub Action runs the loops; OpenRouter runs the calls. The Action's run step holds OPEN_ROUTER_KEY and ELASTIC_CLOUD, the Elastic deployment's superuser password: 'a disposable password on a temporary account with no confidential data' (Fringe abp/policies.json, Dinis 01:44 UTC); after the demo it becomes a write-only key for swarm-* (architect.1's design §4). A separate job writes and attests the result.

steps.caption: Can any of them reach Gmail or Calendar? No: those are not connected where they run. The one line today is the Action to a disposable Elastic. Don't hope the agent behaves. Make the dangerous thing unreachable.

scenes.title: Keys that live for one run
scenes.say: E5: the operator key signs the code and the policy, and certifies a key made for one execution. Each key's birth and death is in the record.

steps.label: the keys

card.title: A key on everything, for one run

steps.caption: The operator key lived 314 ms, in memory only. One gap, said plainly: the execution key spent 213 ms in a file other root processes could read.

scenes.title: A key born inside the run
scenes.say: E9, the sequel to E5: the execution key is made inside the harnessed process and dies with it (1.5 s here, only because the unit waits for the neighbour test). No file, no key row in the policy, no credential-like names in the child's environment. A root process next door found no key file, but could open the process's memory: the next row is a separate uid. E10 then ran the unit as its own uid: another uid is refused; root and the same uid outside the sandbox are not; root under its own policy is. Yama is not available on this kernel.
scenes.cue: Safe from files. Not yet from a root neighbour; that is the next row.

scenes.title: A handover through a vault
scenes.say: A real handover, 01:46:30 to 01:56:43 UTC: relay.1 hands a task to relay.2, which hands its result to relay.3. 21 steps, 3 agents, 3 keys. The data travels encrypted through vaults; Git only ever holds keys sealed to the next agent and a public summary. Step 16 is the beat: relay.3 tries to open a key sealed to relay.2.

steps.label: the four places

card.title: Where the data is, step by step

steps.caption: Four places data can be: on the network, decrypted in an agent's memory, encrypted in a vault, public in Git.

steps.label: relay.1 hands over

card.title: Where the data is, step by step

steps.caption: relay.1 reads the public data, puts it in a vault, and seals the vault's key to relay.2's key alone. Git gets the sealed key and a signed task.

steps.label: relay.2 works

card.title: Where the data is, step by step

steps.caption: relay.2 checks the signature, unseals the key, works on the data in its own memory, and hands its result on the same way.

steps.label: relay.3 tries the wrong key

card.title: Where the data is, step by step

steps.caption: relay.3 tries to open the key sealed to relay.2. Decryption failed; nothing written. The seal is the control, not a rule.

steps.label: the public summary

card.title: Where the data is, step by step

steps.caption: relay.3 opens its own, checks the result, and publishes aggregates only. Private input in Git: never.

scenes.title: The wrong agent gets nothing
scenes.say: handover h002 (real): relay.1 sealed the vault key to relay.3 but addressed the task to relay.2. relay.2's key cannot open it: that is reach. relay.3 could open it and did not, because it was not the named reader: that is behaviour.

steps.label: the wrong key

card.title: h002: a key sealed to someone else

steps.caption: relay.2's key cannot open a key sealed to relay.3: refused, nothing written, the vault never fetched. That is reach: it cannot.

steps.label: could, and didn't

card.title: h002: a key sealed to someone else

steps.caption: relay.3 could open it, and did not: it was not the reader named in the task. That is behaviour, not reach. We show it; we don't rely on it.

scenes.title: Blocked inside the harness
scenes.say: handover h003 (real), held back with the findings: inside SHarness, verify, unseal, clone through the door, compute and sign all ran; the vault write then failed (a system file denied; the door carries no credential, so HTTP 401: harness.1's F6, F7, drafted, not filed). Outcome: failed.

steps.label: the handover

card.title: h003: the harness held; the work did not finish

steps.caption: The harness held. The work didn't finish, and the record says why: one system file denied, one credential the door can't carry. Closed as failed, not worked around.

scenes.cue: The harness stopped the attacker we imagined, and the job we needed. Both are in the log.

scenes.title: Who controls what they can do?
scenes.say: Governance: the honest line is that most rules observe and three enforce. That was a choice.

card.title: Who controls what they can do?
lines: Deny by default: one written grant per role and agent (45 agents in abp/policies.json v0.4.1).

lines.text: 12 core rules · 3 enforced · the rest observed

lines: Enforced by a hook: push to dev only (R5), never print a key (R8), commit only under your own name (R9).
The rest observe and log, by Dinis's choice: we learn first, and the log shows what each rule would have blocked.

scenes.title: A licence that lapses when the reach changes
scenes.say: A licence to operate, granted against this container's measured reach. Then a tool is connected (simulated: a Gmail MCP server). The fingerprint changes, the licence suspends itself, and the next actions wait for a person.
scenes.cue: The licence was for the world as it was. When the world changes, the licence waits for a person.

steps.label: granted
